title: Lamentations 2:20–22
context: Zion answers with a closing appeal to the LORD: “Look, LORD, and see to whom you have done thus!” She asks whether women should eat their offspring, the children they had held and bounced on their knees, and whether priest and prophet should be killed in the sanctuary of the Lord. Youth and old man lie in the streets; her young women and young men have fallen by the sword; she says the LORD has killed and slaughtered, and not pitied, in the day of his anger. Terrors have been called as to a solemn assembly; no one escaped in the day of the LORD’s anger; the enemy has consumed those she had cared for and brought up. The question about the women and their children is stated only as the verse states it, soberly and briefly, without elaboration. The slain in the sanctuary and in the streets require the same restraint. This is a lament’s last appeal in the chapter, not a place for a lecture, and not a new soteriological contrast. Wrath, grief, and the address to the LORD remain shared ground. 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52 may be named by reference for the fall of the city and the house, without harmonizing.

verses.text: “Look, LORD, and see to whom you have done thus! Should the women eat their offspring, the children that they held and bounced on their knees? Should the priest and the prophet be killed in the sanctuary of the Lord?
verses.arminianNotes:
Zion says, “Look, LORD, and see to whom you have done thus!” She asks, “Should the women eat their offspring, the children that they held and bounced on their knees? Should the priest and the prophet be killed in the sanctuary of the Lord?” The questions are her appeal, and they are left in their own words, stated once, soberly, and without any added description. The ruined sanctuary and the famine-grief belong to that same brief report.

Arminian readers hear a real prayer that the LORD would look at what has been done, including these things the verse names, a plea that does not need to be filled out beyond the text.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same “Look, LORD, and see,” and the same two questions, as Zion’s closing address, to be reported as she asks them and not enlarged.

Shared ground: she asks the LORD to see. The appeal is kept brief and does not sensationalize what the verse already says with terrible plainness.

verses.text: “The youth and the old man lie on the ground in the streets. My virgins and my young men have fallen by the sword. You have killed them in the day of your anger. You have slaughtered, and not pitied.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The youth and the old man lie on the ground in the streets. My virgins and my young men have fallen by the sword.” She then says the LORD has killed them in the day of his anger, and has slaughtered, and not pitied. Age and youth are both in the streets; the sword has taken the young women and young men she calls hers. The report should remain sober and without added scene. The “not pitied” matches earlier lines in the chapter and is still the language of lament.

Arminian readers hear Zion ascribe the slaughter to the LORD’s anger, and still speak to him, a grief that covers the whole population in the streets, which the poem is right to tell in short, hard sentences.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same lying in the streets, the fallen young women and young men, and the word that the LORD has killed and slaughtered in the day of his anger, and not pitied.

Shared ground: the streets hold the dead, and the day is the day of his anger. Pastoral restraint continues to govern the notes.

verses.text: “You have called, as in the day of a solemn assembly, my terrors on every side. There was no one that escaped or remained in the day of the LORD’s anger. My enemy has consumed those whom I have cared for and brought up.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You have called, as in the day of a solemn assembly, my terrors on every side.” No one escaped or remained in the day of the LORD’s anger. “My enemy has consumed those whom I have cared for and brought up.” The feast-day image is now a summoning of terrors; the enemy has consumed the ones she had raised. The chapter ends in that loss. The cared-for and brought-up should be named only as she names them, without expansion.

Arminian readers hear a last first-person cry: terrors called as to an assembly, none escaping, and the enemy consuming those she raised, a close that leaves the grief in the LORD’s hearing.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same calling of terrors, the day of the LORD’s anger with no one remaining, and the enemy’s consuming of those she had cared for and brought up, as Zion’s final words in the chapter.

Shared ground: the unit ends as an appeal and a lament, not as a resolved argument. Both traditions can remain with her at this close.
